utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. I would remind you, Mr. Coo, that the affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I guess the first thing I'd like to do this morning, Your Honour, is tender 02845.01, which is the list of exhibits in Mr. Coo's provenance report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The list, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01287.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, there are two other general types of documents or categories of documents that I'd like to address with you while you're here. One involves VJ collegium minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could have 00928 on screen to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with those meeting minutes from your work at the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know how those were received in the possession of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to check my -- the spreadsheet I prepared, but I believe we got them in response to an RFA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you review those minutes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during the Milutinovic trial, did you follow when those minutes were discussed with various witnesses, including several of the attendees of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you aware that they were admitted into evidence in the Milutinovic trial?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of any challenge or claim that they were not authentic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I don't know if you can see that on your screen now.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Is this the same format in which they all appeared to be printed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you need to look at any of the rest of it to familiarise yourself with it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I recognise this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we, for a moment, though, look at page 2 in both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And here we have a list of those present at this particular meeting. Was it -- is that standard formatting for these minutes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have any more questions about that. Your Honour, I would like to tender this one 00928, and there are a series of these. It runs through 0941, and these are all meetings I think from December 1998 through -- and up to the beginning of the war. There's only one during the war, I think it's on April 9th, 1999, but they were all received pursuant to the same RFA, they're all in the same format, and they were all testified about by many of the attendees of these meetings during the Milutinovic trial. And we would offer them in their entirety, although there are portions in the meeting clearly where subject matters are being discussed that may not be pertinent to your final findings in this case, but we feel that you need to have the entire meetings to have the context of what's being discussed, to understand the inter-relationships between the speakers and the events about which they're talking about. Certainly at the end of the case when we file our final brief we will be directing your attention to those particular most pertinent points from our point of view, but that's our proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it these are not on the list we were using yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, they were not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They were not. Is there any objection to these, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was just about to stand up, and I must say that I'm a little bit surprised by this gesture by my colleague, Mr. Hannis, because we were not quite specifically informed what would be in the announcement. So I'm a little bit surprised about this type of use of this document. I didn't have any time to look in detail exactly what it's about. I assume it is something that I've already seen and read, but at this point I really am unable to say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may make a suggestion. I would propose to provide a list to the Registry of those exhibits that I intend to offer, these VJ collegium minutes, and certainly allow Mr. Djordjevic time to review if there are any particular ones that he objects to and respond in writing if that's necessary or helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that could be the way most usefully for us to take, Mr. Hannis. There will be -- if when he reviews them, if there are concerns of Mr. Djordjevic he's going to put them in writing to the documents that you were dealing with yesterday, and this could be included in that exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, I am not opposed to that, but I would just like to point out to the Chamber that this should not be something that becomes a practice. Documents that are going to be used should be provided in advance. I'm going to ask for two weeks for the bar table submission, and at the same time, since Mr. Hannis is already talking about this, that after the conclusion of the examination-in-chief of this witness we be provided with a final list so that the Defence can then know precisely what it is dealing with in terms of the documents that were being used. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I understand it, Mr. Djordjevic, you have the list from yesterday that has been the subject of specific evidence in some respects, and there are now tendered this and a number of other minutes of this same body, the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff. So that should be at the moment the totality of the documents. There may be more which Mr. Hannis is going to deal with now, but we'll move on. The motion for them to be received in evidence will be dealt with when we've had any objections in writing that Mr. Djordjevic wishes to put forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do want to indicate that although these VJ collegium documents were not on the initial notification concerning Mr. Coo, we did notify the Defence by e-mail Wednesday, near the end of the day, that I would be addressing these with Mr. Coo as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The last general category of documents, Mr. Coo, I wanted to address with you are RFAs, requests for assistance, which we talked about a little bit before. The first one I'd like you to have a look at is 02335. I don't know if you will have seen this particular one before or not, but in terms of your general practice, does this look like the -- look like -- is it in the format in which you would typically receive a response to an RFA request?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see that the first paragraph says the Ministry of Foreign Affairs presents its compliments -- I think you told us yesterday that these were generally processed by the MFA, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This one, Your Honours, is brought to your attention because on page 2, if we could turn to that in the B/C/S and English, it's a response to several RFAs. And on page 2 you'll see reference to ICTY request 1098 regarding Mala and Velika Krusa. It has a list of names of several individuals and then describes what information MUP had about these particular persons. And on page 4 of the English, if we could, the other one that we wanted to bring to your attention is the portion that responds to ICTY request, near the bottom of the page, ICTY request 1105 with the names of three individuals in connection with Bela Crkva. I'm sorry, in the B/C/S I think we need to go one page further, and we have to go to the bottom of the English. Thank you. And then if I can explain the process further, if we could have a look at 02855. While that's coming up I'd like to tender 02335.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there going to be a series of these or a number that is quite separate?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The one that's on the screen and one more following -- the first three of these are related to each other, they're part of a chain, but I don't know if it's -- it may be more useful to have separate numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, this will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01288.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, now on the screen is 02855, you recognise this format?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Djordjevic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence can note that the B/C/S does not -- that the B/C/S does not correspond to the English text. What we see on the screen is not what my learned friend is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That seems to be the correct one now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you see that, Mr. Coo, this, what's on the screen right now says it's a reminder RFA 1315. You recognise this format?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you explain what reminder RFAs were about?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are issued when the dead-line for the original RFA has passed without a response being received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you see in the text of this one it makes reference to an earlier request on the 15th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to another page in English, I'm not sure which page it is in the sequence. I think it's the one we had up on the screen first in English. Yes. And if we could find the corresponding page in the B/C/S. I apologise that they weren't sequenced correctly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is a problem in that there are only two B/C/S pages in the e-court system, whereas the document in English has five pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is a problem. Could I see the other page of the B/C/S, or is that it on the screen now? Well, Your Honours, I'm afraid I'm going to have to abandon ship on this one for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you want the witness to comment at all on the content of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, if I may, and then I will attempt to locate the B/C/S translation of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, can you describe for us what's on the screen now in terms of the general format?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the general format of our requests for assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Government of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see in the fourth paragraph of the text it makes reference to a response T-166-22/2006/9. The persons in Annex A were identified as holding positions within the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm afraid that in this way we're going to violate the rights of the accused to defence because this is a document that he cannot understand, perceive, or follow. And because of that I'm concerned that my learned friend, Mr. Hannis, was correct when he said that for now he might need to leave this document aside. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is occurring, Mr. Djordjevic, will not involve any violation of any rights of your client. You know, as well as we, that many times in this trial it has been necessary to deal with a document usually put forward by a member of the Defence team that is in one of the two main languages we are using and not the other. We have dealt with the document and then held it until a translation is available, and then when that has occurred the document has been exhibited. What is happening here is exactly that: A document is being shown to the witness, the witness is commenting on it, the witness's comments are being translated to your client. This document will not be received as an exhibit unless and until there is a proper translation. And I think in that way your client will not be in any way disadvantaged and we can move on, which is the important thing we are trying to do at the moment with a document which is no more than a formal request. Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could go to the next page in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We have Annex A to this request which has a list of names, and it makes reference to a prior request numbered 1098 and 1105 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which I would indicate to Your Honours were names that we saw in the exhibit prior to this one, which now has Exhibit Number P1288. And you'll see in the body of this request that it is attaching those names and asking for further information from the MUP about these individually identified active and reserve MUP members. So if I could, Your Honour, I would like to have this marked for identification until I can get a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01289, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next if we could look at 02850, and if we could go to the -- we see the name Zvezdan Nikolic on the screen. If we could go to the second page of both B/C/S and English. Your Honours, this is -- Mr. Nikolic is one of the individuals named in the MFI'd document for whom further information was requested and he's one of the individuals named in P1288 from Mala Krusa, listed as being a fireman in the MUP. And we would like to tender this and the remaining documents 02851, 2852, and 02849 as all being part of that same series of requests for information. 2849, 2851, and 2852 relate to other individuals named in the original response to the RFA concerning individuals in Mala Krusa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 02850 will be Exhibit P01290; 65 ter 02851 will be Exhibit P01291; 65 ter 02852 will be Exhibit P01292; and finally, 65 ter 02849 will be Exhibit P01293.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These documents are evidently translated into English, B/C/S, but I wanted to ask since these are accessible documents and they are marked for identification, I think these documents would also need to be marked for identification since they accompany original documents, they're accessories. So they would need to be referenced in view of the fact that we don't have the main document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I haven't followed the point you're making.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I am going to repeat myself. I believe that these documents also need to be marked for identification, since they are accessories to the main documents or an exhibit that has already been MFI'd, because if they get an exhibit number independently now and the previous number that has been marked for identification is never admitted, then these documents are not going to be quite logical -- quite a logical part of the brief, of the case. So I believe that they need to be admitted together with the main document. This is all that I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I must be slow this morning. It's a possibility that I didn't think was real enough to be a problem. We've got a document that simply needs to be translated; once it's translated, it will be exhibited and I think they're in a sequence number. So we'll leave them as they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two more, Mr. Coo, and then I think I'll be finished, 02856. Yes, I'm relieved to see this time we seem to have the translation with this document. This is another RFA, Mr. Coo, and similarly you'll see in the fourth paragraph there's a reference to a response indicating the persons named in Annex A had been previously identified as holding positions within the MUP and requesting further information. Again, this seems to be in the similar -- the usual format of an OTP RFA?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And could we look at Annex A, I think it's the third page in the English. And I don't know if there's a translation of this list of names -- yes, we do have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'd like to tender 02856.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01294.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And lastly 02857. I see we have English on both my pages on the screen. I hope there's a B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We don't seem to be having a lot of luck with your documents, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not any good luck, Your Honour. I think if we could have the English that was previously on the right-hand screen now put up on the left-hand screen it will match the B/C/S that's on the right-hand side now. And that's what I'd like to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Coo, you -- can you see this response, does it appear to be in the typical format from the Government of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, these named individuals were persons that we saw in the first exhibit, P1288 -- 1288 connected with Bela -- with Orahovac and Bela Crkva. These individuals were also named by witnesses who testified in this case, by first name, Lulzim Vejsa mentioned these individuals, and I think the witness Sami Parashumti also mentioned these individuals in Exhibits 1290 through 1293. Those individuals identified in the RFA responses were mentioned by the witnesses from Mala Krusa, Lutfi Ramadani and Mehmet Krasniqi and also John Sweeny in terms of relevance. I want to bring that to your attention. And I don't recall, if I haven't tendered this one, I would like to tender it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You haven't moved. I notice two things about the B/C/S -- well, one thing about the B/C/S, it does not include the last paragraph of the English, and the second thing is that the English is labelled as an unofficial translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would move to submit the B/C/S for an official translation; and you're right, I don't see the additional paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's merely a complement, but if we're to look at a translation, or have a translation, it ought to be, A, official; B, correct. I think I'm doing your job, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you for that. First of all, I would like to say that you're absolutely right, that the last passage is missing from the translation; on the other hand, I don't see the purpose of telling the witness which witnesses in these proceedings have mentioned the people mentioned herein. This witness is not speaking about the contents of the document; he's speaking only about the authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Judges, to assist us in seeing how these documents are relevant in the case. We will mark for identification at the moment, Mr. Hannis, and I'm afraid you must attend to the problems that we've identified. And could I also draw to your attention that the way these have been provided and loaded into e-court is extremely confusing. And I would suggest that for everybody's ease of reference that they be properly matched in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take your words to heart, Your Honour, and we will try to do better in the future. Oh, I see the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01295, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I should indicate, Your Honour, I think K74 also mentioned these individuals. Let me ask Mr. Coo a question concerning these RFAs because I'm not clear on one thing about the translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, when the OTP received responses to RFAs, in what language did we receive it? Did we receive it only in B/C/S, or did Serbia send us a translation of the B/C/S document that they were sending us as well, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who provided the translation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have some questions. I would just kindly ask you to bear with me to prepare myself for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Coo. I name is Dragoljub Djordjevic and I represent the accused in these proceedings. I have some questions for you along the lines which will lead us to establishing the level of authenticity of the documents that Mr. Hannis has been asking you about, and I may go even a step further. Mr. Coo, tell me, when did you finally stop being engaged by the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: 3rd of March, 2008, was my last day of work at the ICTY, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Coo, what I would like to hear about is your formal education. You said that you have a degree in psychology. When did you graduate?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I graduated in 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And then you joined the Canadian Army. What kind of jobs did you perform in the army?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined the Canadian Army as an intelligence officer. After the intelligence -- six-month intelligence officers course, I was assigned to national intelligence headquarters where I was a desk officer on the -- on a -- where my role was the study of the strategic rocket forces in the former Soviet Union. I then became a watch officer in the watch centre in national defence headquarters which was responsible for 24/7 monitoring of events in the world. My next job was to be in charge of an imagery analysis team at the national level, which also incorporated other sources of information. I was then posted to the 1st Canadian Division Headquarters and served there as the head of the intelligence collection and analysis cell within the division's intelligence company. During that posting I was sent to -- on a tour, a seven-month tour, in Bosnia in 1996, finishing in 1997. I came back to the 1st Canadian Division Headquarters and became the adjutant to the commanding officer of the intelligence company. Subsequently moved to Calgary, leaving the regular force and taking up an appointment as a reserve officer with the 6th Intelligence Company which is based in western Canada which is a subunit of a reserve brigade, and that's where I completed my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in 1996 and 1997 you toured Bosnia and Herzegovina. What did you do there, what kind of jobs?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My official title was G2 operations within the multi-national brigade headquarters, which was centred on a Canadian brigade. We had components from other nationalities in the brigade headquarters. Our area of responsibility covered from Prijedor over to Bihac and down to Drvar, primarily the area of the 5th Corps, the Bosnian Army's 5th Corps. We -- my function was to analyse the information that was being collected on activities in our area of responsibility and to be responsible for the team of intelligence analysts and operators for the production of intelligence reports, including a daily intelligence report, on security issues, political issues, and any issue concerning the mandate of the brigade and of interest of the brigade commander within that area of responsibility. So in essence my responsibility was to ensure that the brigade commander was kept informed of what the former warring factions and other entities were doing within his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. What was your rank when you left the Canadian Army?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Captain. Tell me, please, did you leave with some work characteristics, with a reference of any kind?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand the question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I can assume, but I believe that a person who leaves the army is given a letter of reference or a "to whom it may concern" letter stating the evaluation of that person's work. I assume the same applies to the Canadian Army. So my question is whether you were given such a letter of reference with the evaluation of your work?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no letter of reference. We had annual assessments, but upon leaving -- although I can recollect receiving certainly not a letter but certification that I'd left with good standing, but it didn't go into any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Coo, once you left the Canadian Army, where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My next job after the Canadian Army was the position of an analyst in the Military Analysis Team at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you land the job immediately, or did you do some other things in the OTP before you became an analyst? Did you work as an investigator, for example?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no association with the OTP or the ICTY until I arrived late May 1999 to become an analyst.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And after that stint, did you then work as an investigator?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never had the title "investigator." I've perhaps done in the ICTY what an investigator does at times, but that wasn't my primary function. For example, I've taken part in the interviews of witnesses, but my primary function wasn't that of investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But the fact that you did that as well, de jure you had another posting. Will you agree with me that that's true?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't describe it as another posting. I had varied responsibilities or varied use was made of my knowledge within the OTP, and that included taking part in the interviews of witnesses, but I was never formally considered or even de jure considered an investigator. I had no -- never made an application to be an investigator or was considered -- called an investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The interpretation was bad. I didn't say that this was your other posting; I said something completely different. What I said was this: De jure you had your job; however, de facto in part what you did was also the job of an investigator. I never said that that was your other posting. Let's make things clear here. My next question, however, is this: Did you participate in the interviewing of the accused in the related cases, such as the Milosevic case, the Milutinovic case, the Limaj case, and I believe that there is another Kosovo case, did you participate in interviewing the accused or whether you were present when the accused in the -- these cases were being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only interviewed or was present during the interviews of accused in the Milutinovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, which of the accused did you interview personally? Maybe I can be of assistance. If you can't remember, I can jog your memory by giving you the names of all the accused.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I took part in the interviews of Generals Pavkovic, Lazarevic, and Lukic. I think those are the only three that I'd -- that I was -- three accused with whom I was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you participate in interviews with the witnesses who appeared in some of the cases?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, again in -- primarily in the Milosevic and the Milutinovic case. I don't recall ever interviewing any witnesses in the Limaj or Haradinaj case -- in fact, I wasn't involved in the Haradinaj case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the names of some of the witnesses, some of whom have already testified in this case?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember some of the names. It would probably be easier for me to confirm if given names, but I certainly remember interviewing VJ Generals Djakovic, Vasiljevic; MUP General Radosavljevic; and there were a number of other witnesses who don't spring to mind at the moment but I'd certainly remember them if prompted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were you present during the interview of General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, were you there all the time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic was interviewed a number of times, including for the other components of the Milosevic case. I wasn't involved in all of those interviews. I recall being involved in -- certainly in one lengthy interview, possibly a second time, but there were many others that I wasn't involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember having interviewed Zarko Brakovic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He was a PJP commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in the interviews with Richard Ciaglinski, John Drewienkiewicz, with Shaun Byrnes as well?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, with all three of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Coo, when did you start working on documents related to this or these cases?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I began working on the documents as soon as I started my work at the ICTY at the end of May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you perceive yourself as an expert for military and security issues and analysis? Do you consider yourself a military and security analyst?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider myself a military analyst. That's the title I had here. The title of "expert" I wouldn't want to bestow on myself; that's for others to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that at the beginning of your military career you took a short intelligence course. Did you also attend some higher military schools where you would be dealing with military theory, analysis, philosophy, war doctrine, and similar disciplines?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that would be handled at staff college. I didn't attend staff college. I attended an intermediate tactics course which dealt with company-level tactics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How long was the course that you attended?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic intelligence officer's course in the Canadian Army at the time was -- began in January, I believe, and finished in June 1989. The intermediate tactics course was a one-month course. I did do a number of shorter courses during my career, for example, a course in indications and warnings, which is an effort to predict in a systematic way enemy intentions and activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Before you joined the ICTY, did you author an article, a professional article, dealing with military analytical issues? Did you publish any papers with that topic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. All my publications were intelligence reports and classified intelligence reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, can you please tell me, if when you arrived at The Hague, if you attended any type of course or attend any type of training that focuses on the maintaining and the preservation of archives and so on, since I understood that you did nothing like that before you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never attended such a course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if as part of the tasks for the OTP and for this Tribunal you acquainted yourself in detail with the structure of the Army of Yugoslavia, and in accordance with that with the manner in which it archived its documents during the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the main functions I had was to understand the structure of the Army of Yugoslavia during the period of interest, and we also sought through various means to understand the documentation that it produced and where that documentation would be kept or archived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And how did you learn about the manner of the archiving of material in the Army of Yugoslavia? My specific question is: Was this through conversations with the pertinent people, or was it by reading laws, books of regulations, or any other sources?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any single document which enlightened us fully about the archiving. It -- we asked witnesses, for example, VJ officers who would be familiar with it. We -- I noted in some documents references to archiving. We finally obtained the rules of office administration and correspondence for the VJ, which made reference to archiving regulations. And there was a general understanding, also assisted by our leadership research team in the Office of the Prosecutor, which was -- did have people familiar with archiving that there were state archives within the former Yugoslavia and, as I said, general understanding that militaries do -- are required to archive their documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When did you get this military archiving regulations document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the specific date. It was -- I believe it was during the later stages of the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if you acquainted yourself in the same way with the structure of the Ministry of the Interior; and if not, did you inform yourself about the way of maintaining the Ministry of the Interior archives; and if you did, again I would like to ask you what sources did you use for that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same approach was taken with the Ministry of the Interior. We were less successful in obtaining documentation which would enlighten us about the archiving procedures and similarly with witnesses, and in the end we never had the same understanding of MUP archiving that we had with the VJ's archiving system. But again, we operated from the -- or I operated from the approach that there were state archives and there's laws, regulations, mandating states to archive official documentation. So we certainly made efforts to seek access to archives and to seek documents that we believed would be in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what a document register is?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with document registers and we also reviewed document registers eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to go back to a question. When you interviewed General Vasiljevic, did you interview him in the capacity of a witness or suspect at that time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that General Vasiljevic was a suspect in connection to the Croatian part of the Milosevic indictment. I don't remember for certain whether we interviewed him as a suspect when interviewing him about Kosovo, but I know for certain that he was a suspect in one component of the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did it ever occur to you that the forensic investigation of the archived material that you received and the documents that you obtained yourselves from non-government organisations, institutions, and individuals for the purposes of checking the -- these documents needed to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the potential for documents to be forged or modified in some way. The capacity and the ability to justify a forensic -- a full forensic examination, including handwriting analysis or analysis of the font, for example, for every single document just wasn't there. And I also didn't feel that it was required for most of the documentation that I was reviewing because I -- I found that it -- much of it could be corroborated by documentation obtained independently and the content of the documentation was often so innocuous that I couldn't imagine somebody going to the effort of forging or modifying it. And in addition, there were also official stamps and -- for the most part and signature blocks. So I didn't feel very concerned about a requirement to conduct a full forensic analysis of the documents, with a very small number of exceptions which I don't recall ever using in my reports anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any documents that were investigated or tested in this particular way?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we did request some forensic analysis, handwriting analysis, for example, of some documents used in or which we had connected to the Kosovo cases. I can't recall the specifics. There was one document in the Milosevic case which was a list of Albanians or Siptars to be killed. And certainly in the Milutinovic case and in my reports, that document was not referred to. We were very skeptical of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any kind of forensic findings? I'm asking you this in reference to perhaps a request for handwriting analysis of a particular document. Did you receive any results of analysis or not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I believe the OTP received some reports from the Netherlands Forensics Institute on handwriting analysis, but I don't remember receiving any specifically myself or being involved in the interaction with the Forensics Institute or study of those particular documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who else was entrusted with analysing the documents in the OTP? Weren't you the sole person responsible for that? This is what we have been led to believe, at least regarding the analysis of police and army documents. Can you tell us the name if there is such a person?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A number of people reviewed documents for a variety of purposes, investigators, other analysts, research officers looking at the more political level of documents. For the purposes of writing the reports that I wrote, I was responsible for reviewing those documents for incorporation into my reports. Many of those same documents would have been also reviewed by other people for other purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But you told me that you issued requests for certain analysis to be conducted for specific documents, handwriting analysis; am I correct to understand that that was so?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think I said that, but if I did that's incorrect. I never requested handwriting analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Because then that is the right answer then because you said something so we all understood something different from what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we ask the usher now to put two documents up on the screen, and I would like to first place the Serbian, B/C/S, originals, side by side. This is 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I think that is P887. And 65 ter document number 01722, D -- this is D204, the first one was 65 ter 01460. All right. All right, that is the first document. Can we now look at the second document. [In English] Please. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you look at these two documents, even though they're in B/C/S - and you said you dealt with examining the authenticity of the document - are you familiar with the format of this document or not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the formats of both look familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do these documents seem to be original documents, authentic documents, to you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At face value they look authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask to zoom in on document P887 -- actually, to zoom the stamps on both documents, the first one, for example, the command of the 3rd Army. Could we zoom in on that. It's in the top left-hand corner at -- in the heading of the document. Thank you. And can you please zoom in the same place on the document, the text there is typed, but then there is something that is entered by hand. Yes, precisely. That's the part.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The first document has number 872-94/2, and bears the date the 19th of April, 1999. You can see that, right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The second document bears the same number 872-94/1 and bears the date the 20th of April, 1999; you can see that, right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: These are two separate documents, the documents that we see on the left-hand side was signed by General Ojdanic, and the one on the right-hand side was signed by General Pavkovic. The left document is a telegram or an order signed by General Ojdanic, and the right document is an order signed by General Pavkovic. Would you agree with me that in 1999 General Ojdanic was the one who could issue orders to General Pavkovic and that General Pavkovic was subordinated to General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It's clear that on the 19th of April General Ojdanic wrote the document, this is 1999, and that on the 20th of April General Pavkovic in relation to this document wrote his document. How do you explain the fact that document that is the earlier document bears the marking /2, the original document, and the later document is marked with the number /1? Does that bring any doubts in your mind in reference to this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does look odd. I think I would have to see the full translations to make a definitive -- offer a definitive opinion on these.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to ask to have the versions that are translated of these documents placed on the monitor side by side, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the first sentence in the first paragraph: "Pursuant to the order, strictly confidential ..."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So this refers to the previous document that bears the number /2, and this one bears the marking /1. So may I hear your comment on this now, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the one on the left is the General Staff's order on subordination of the MUP to the VJ issued on the 18th of April, 1999, that it has a stamp on the top of the 3rd Army with the reference number 872-94/2, dated the 19th of April, 1999. I don't know what that stamp is doing there. It may be the stamp to indicate receipt of the General Staff's order. The document on the right I understand to be the 3rd Army's response to the order of the General Staff which is issued on the 20th of April, 1999, and given the strictly confidential number 872-94/1. Why there's a discrepancy between the stamp at the top of the -- 3rd Army stamp at the top of the left-hand document and the one on the right, I don't know. 94, by which I mean 94/2, preceding in date 94/1. It seems odd. It could be a transcription error, but I have no explanation for what the reason is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There is no typing mistake for the simple reason that you saw the originals and you saw what it says in the originals. Second, I am wondering that you are wondering about this stamp. Don't you know that this is a register number, not a receipt stamp. Do you know what a receipt stamp looks like used by the Army of Yugoslavia, it says "received" at such and such a time. Do you know, did you ever see such a stamp before? Actually, we are on this topic and you are an expert on this. Did you know that this is a register number not a receipt stamp?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen the receipt stamps on documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So why are you wondering? You're saying perhaps it was received then, but this is actually the document register number of the basic -- the main document. All right, thank you. Well, anyway, something is odd here, something is not clear here, all of this is used in these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to permit that these two documents be admitted side by side if possible, to have the two English documents admitted side by side both and then the B/C/S versions of the documents also, if it's possible to do it this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are they not already exhibits? I thought you said that the first of them is Exhibit P887 and the second Exhibit D204.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, and this other one is D204. I just thought for the sake of being practical to place these two exhibits side by side in the electronic evidence data, even though they're already admitted. I don't know if this is necessary or not, but I thought perhaps for the sake of being practical I suggested that. I don't know if so far the practice was like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... we don't need to attempt to place them side by side unless at some other stage we're having to compare the two again, and then it's a matter of just doing as has been done here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then in future I will not be making any suggestions like this then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, you said that documents were collected in several ways. You referred to that in our report, but let's go by order.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is asked to read more slowly the title of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has already been admitted. This has already been admitted as evidence. And I'm not going to refer to it in particular or ask for the document to be placed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the first way of gathering the documents was going on a mission to seek the documents. Is it correct that the OTP immediately after the signing of the Kumanovo Agreement and NATO's entry in Kosovo set off to compile documents or collect documents?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The OTP sent teams to Kosovo as soon as the war ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was this done according to a specific plan or of -- with the aims of a specific plan or goal in terms of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or was it done also in terms of the Albanians and the KLA in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not clear, Your Honours, on what the -- what it means by "in terms of the Albanians and the KLA," but there was a plan - I wasn't privy to the planning, I just essentially just arrived at the ICTY at the time. But certainly a plan to send teams to Kosovo as soon as the war ended to visit sites where MUP and VJ had headquarters and also the political institutions in Kosovo, the municipal headquarters, for example. So teams were sent to such facilities to look for documents and to seize them before anybody else did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that this would be an appropriate time for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will take the first break now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coo, when NATO forces and IFOR entered after the Kumanovo Agreement, did anybody deal with the crimes that were committed by Albanians against the non-Albanian population of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know specifically what NATO and KFOR did in regard to the crimes, such crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about the OTP, I'm asking about the ICTY. Immediately after NATO came, did the ICTY or anybody in the ICTY deal with the crimes committed by Albanians against the non-Albanian population of Kosovo? That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I see. I don't know when the OTP's -- when the OTP began its investigations into the crimes alleged by -- against the Kosovo Albanians. I worked on the -- and supported the team that was tasked solely with the crimes falling under the Milosevic indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I can see in the record against the Kosovo Albanians [In English] -- against the Kosovo Albanians. [Interpretation] My question was as follows: Against the non-Albanian population by the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not -- Your Honours, I'm aware of any specific investigation conducted at that time in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And subsequently was anything done at any later stage as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crimes committed by Albanians against the non-Albanian population, my understanding has formed the basis for the Limaj and Haradinaj indictments; and the team that was dealing with those, the investigation team that was dealing with that aspect of Kosovo, I wasn't working with that team. So they may well have investigated other crimes and considered other indictments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, if I understand you properly, you did not deal with any documentation that was collected with regard to the war crimes committed by Albanians? Am I right in assuming that? As a military analyst and as an expert, you didn't deal with that documentation as an expert of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I wouldn't want to phrase it so -- in such a constrained way or specific way. The documentation that I reviewed for the task that I was assigned meant that I came across a lot of documentation that may have eventually made its way into or could be considered as documentation that was relevant to crimes committed by Albanians against non-Albanians. I can't remember the specifics or specific examples, but I would have in the process of conducting electronic searches of our evidence database, for example, have come across far more than simply VJ orders or activities of the VJ and MUP in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That was not my question, sir. Tell me, from the very outset was there a unique pattern governing the collection of documents on Kosovo? Did you have a regulation or an instruction as to how to deal with the collected documents?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents collected in Kosovo had to be processed in accordance with the OTP's procedures on handling of evidence. So maintenance of the chain of custody, consideration of documentation which may have had exculpatory information in it. So certainly if we came across information or any of the teams coming across information that was deemed to be relevant, either inculpatory or exculpatory, it had to be handled in accordance with our OTP provisions on the handling of evidence. So it was registered and entered into our evidence system. The way that documents were collected at that time, immediately after the war, was that the -- there wasn't much time to get to the documents before the potential of them disappearing or being taken by others or destroyed by the weather, because a lot of them were in destroyed buildings, occurred. So there was some urgency and not every document could be reviewed in great detail. So in that respect a lot of documentation that may have had no relevance at all to any cases was collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You will then agree with me that as a matter of fact there was an agreed process when it comes to the collection of documents, but there was no regulation governing the mission to search for documents? There was nothing formal in that respect?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no standing regulation for -- there was no standing regulation for the collection of documents in -- on these document-collection missions in Kosovo, no. There were -- there were instructions to the team members of the document-collection missions on how to collect and process these documents and where to go, what we were looking for, and how to ensure that the regulations for handling evidence were maintained, such as maintenance of chain of custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for the digression that I'm going to make. When you were collecting documents and when you analysed the documents originating from the Army of Yugoslavia, did you collate the numbers that you found in the heading of the documents with the book in which the documents were recorded? Was that an approach that you adopted in cross-checking the documents that you collected?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That didn't occur until we had access to the archives of the Army of Yugoslavia, which came much later. I believe it was in 2006 that we finally gained access to archives, and at that point we had access to the registers. Before then we didn't have any access to the registers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Once you had access, did you back-checked the documents that you collected previously? Did you collate the numbers you found in the headings of the documents with the books in which the documents were recorded? Did you do that ex post?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We couldn't do this retroactively in a systematic fashion. We checked some of the more important documents in the registers of the archives by register number, by date, by document title and content. But for the most part those archive missions were to seek documents that we didn't already have, and there was a limited time to conduct those missions. So the approach taken was to review the registers, identify documents that were likely to be of interest based on the dates and the titles, and to request to see those documents in the archive. We would review them in the archive, and if in fact they were of interest we had to come back here and then submit an RFA saying that on the basis of the archive mission we would like to be given these documents. And it would take a few months minimum to be given those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that there was some documents that you deemed to be very relevant and that you checked them and collated them with the books. After that, did you somehow mark those documents as having been double-checked in that way, or did you not do that at all?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no specific marking of double-checking because we -- the protocol agreed to for archive access was that we would be shown the registers in the archive and we could go through the registers. And we would note or list which documents based on the register number we would like, and we also provided some additional detail such as the title and the date. We kept a record of that and we requested it when we came back to the ICTY, and when we received the documentation we did check it against what we had requested to ensure that the response matched the request. In some cases we weren't given all of the documents that we had asked for, but that's the extent to which the double-checking went.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned your concern with regard to the documentation going missing during the mission. How were the buildings secured if they contained archive material and documentation that was collected during the mission?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many of the buildings weren't secured. They -- a number had been destroyed by NATO bombing, a number had already been -- clearly had been -- the documentation had been -- some documentation had been removed, either by the Serb forces leaving Kosovo or by others. But for the most part, we were there so soon after the NATO forces -- KFOR had moved in that it just wasn't possible for all of these buildings to be secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you will agree with me that anybody could access those buildings, any third person could access those buildings and could misuse or misappropriate the documentation in question?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend very much on the building. But yes, there were some buildings which anyone, in theory, could access; some buildings which people certainly couldn't access.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You're saying that the mission was carried out in the following way: The documents would be collected and placed in boxes, which would then be sealed. Tell us something more about the boxes and how the boxes were sealed. This is what I'm reading in your report.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The earliest missions, the documents would be collected with little time to sit in the buildings or elsewhere reviewing them, and they would be put into the -- into boxes with chain of custody forms. The boxes would be taped up, and eventually it was organised that one of the KFOR forces, I believe the Dutch, would fly the boxes under ICTY/OTP escort to maintain chain of custody to The Hague via an airfield in the Netherlands. Later on the missions -- document exploitation missions were able to document and log the documents in the field office in Pristina, and there was a bit more order to the processing of those documents. But in the summer of 1999 it was -- the collection of documents had to be done fairly hastily.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a person in Pristina who was specifically tasked with handling documents and maintaining the chain of custody and was that person appointed by the OTP of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe there was a specific person, certainly not initially. Representatives of the evidence unit were sent to Kosovo to assist with the processing of documents, but it was also incumbent on the analysts and investigators involved in these collection missions to ensure that the chain of custody procedures were maintained.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You're saying that it was recorded where documents were taken, when they were taken, how they were taken. Were the documents recorded on site, where it was taken; or whether it was done subsequently, perhaps in the Pristina office or even later here in Holland?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak for the document missions I was on, one of which I recall in sifting through documents in a large metal container in the former barracks of the 549 Brigade near Prizren. We would select the documents that we considered relevant and collect those together on site, transport them to the office in Pristina, under observation at all times; and the logging of those documents and the packaging of those documents would take place in our field office in Pristina. Eventually the documents collected in the summer 1999 document missions, which we informally called the 85 box collection in the OTP, was - as I noted earlier - flown here by the Royal Netherlands Air Force, under escort of the OTP. I also should add that I -- eventually, as we got more cooperation from Serbia, a large number of those documents that we found in Kosovo became redundant. Some were certainly used as evidence and some were certainly mentioned in my reports, but many were superseded by documents that we got through RFAs and archive missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The end did not sound very clear to me. Are you saying that some of the documents that were found in Kosovo existed in an identical form in the former -- Serbia? Did I understand you well? For example, you found a document in Kosovo and then you come across an identical one in the process of providing legal assistance to the ICTY by the states?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a small number that I'm aware of which fall into that category. I can't think of specifics. So, for example, if a brigade generated a report and sent that report to a higher unit, the version of the report that made it to the higher unit we found in the archive and found the original version of the report in Kosovo, because obviously for many reports there's multiple addressees getting copies. For the most part, however, the documents that we acquired through archive and -- archive missions in Serbia, in Belgrade primarily, and through RFAs, those documents were new documents. The documents we tended to find in Kosovo were 1998 or before, and because of that we determined that the Serb forces had taken -- had certainly done as much of a review as possible and tried to destroy documentation that they weren't taking and taken the most current documentation with them when they withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were some documents of that sort and you also said that some documents were destroyed. Are you speaking from experience? Are you personally aware of some documents having been destroyed? Did that happen sporadically? Do you know anything about that? Could you tell us more?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The condition of some documents that we found in some of the buildings suggested that they -- an effort had been made to destroy them. We had been told in response to some RFAs that some documents had been destroyed. Documents of interest such as the Pristina Corps war diary, the VJ was never able to provide an account of its -- of its fate essentially. So it was never found in an archive, it was never found in Kosovo, and nobody in the Pristina Corps could give us a clear answer about what happened to such an important document. So whether destroyed or lost, it certainly does -- did appear to me that there are examples of that happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your report you state that there were other persons and non-governmental organisations that were allowed to take away documents. What did you mean when you stated that? Which persons did you refer to? Which persons and NGOs were able to take documents away from Kosovo after the entry of NATO and KFOR? I'm sure that you were not speaking about the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any individuals by name or title and I don't know the specifics of organisations -- I also can't say that they were allowed to take documents. But I'm aware of, for example, some witnesses giving documents to investigators that they had found in Kosovo in a variety of buildings. And I'm aware of KFOR seizing or collecting some of the documents that they would come across in some of the buildings and KFOR gave us access to the documents that they had seized.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You very briefly touched upon this in the Milutinovic et al. case, but can you please tell me, what do you know about the presentation of documents by the then-Prime Minister Djindjic regarding General Pavkovic to the Prosecutor at the time, Madam Carla del Ponte?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mistakenly called him president, but Prime Minister Djindjic. The Prosecutor went on a trip to Belgrade, July 2002, I think it was, and was given a number of VJ documents and some Joint Command ones, including minutes of the Joint Command from 1998, in a package, two plastic bags if I recall correctly. And the note taken by her political advisor who was with her receiving these documents which we have in our system records -- I believe, I would have to see it to confirm, but I believe the note states that the documents were put together by General Pavkovic, who was Chief of the General Staff at that time. Many of these documents I had noted were similar to the documents that appeared in that book produced by Vojska which we had bought at the VJ bookshop.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The documents that were presented by Prime Minister Djindjic and General Pavkovic in two bags, was it submitted accompanied by a list and was a receipt given for its receipt by Madam del Ponte, or was it just simply handed over without any kind of receipt being signed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a list of the contents of the two plastic bags. Whether or not there was a receipt, I'm not aware. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The list was drafted later in the OTP of The Hague Tribunal, not at the time when the documents were received; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would have to see this -- the contents of this package, but I believe that the -- there was a list which was compiled by, I presume, the VJ, not by us certainly. We did create a log ourselves later on, but I believe that there was a list with the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think this, or do you know it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to say with a hundred per cent certainty, but I'm quite sure that there was a list provided to us with the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, did you work with these documents once they came to The Hague, specifically those documents, or did somebody else process them in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did work with those documents once they were processed. We did create a log and we submitted them into evidence with the assignment of ERNs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me whether the authenticity of the documents was checked at any point in time and was there any doubt about the veracity of the documents that you received at the time from the person who was the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was obviously a concern to be handed a collection of documents by General Pavkovic without us specifically asking. So that was certainly in the back of our minds. When reviewing the documents I was aware of the need to look out for any signs of tampering or any signs of forgery. There was nothing specific that suggested to me that any particular document had been forged or tampered with. The only thing that was I thought unusual and commented on in my report was the sheer number of orders relating to adherence to the Geneva Conventions and the Laws of War and disciplinary issues. I found it unusual that the VJ would have to issue so many orders in that regard during a relatively short period of time. But we subsequently got some of these same documents through an archive mission in 2006 and the contents were checked against documents received in other ways, and there wasn't, from my recollection, any particular document where we -- where it was questionable -- where the contents were questionable, in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, did you receive the document registers along with that documentation, log-books?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't receive the registers. I would have to see again the collection to see whether or not the lists that I believe came with the package, the bags of documents, was a copy of a register. But specifically, no, we didn't receive the registers. We had requested registers and [Realtime transcript read in error "had"] access to registers in RFAs during the Milosevic trial. And I -- I note in the transcript it says "had access." We requested access. We didn't have access during the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was meant to be my next question actually. Can you please tell me who was the political advisor of Carla del Ponte when Prime Minister Djindjic and General Pavkovic submitted the documents in two plastic bags to Carla del Ponte? What was his name? Of the gentleman?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember who it was in 2002. The name Jean Jacques rings a bell, but I can't be sure that it was him in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been Anton Nikiforov who was another -- working in a political advisor capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Except for what seemed strange to you, such a large number of orders about the respect of the Geneva Conventions and humanitarian law and the laws and customs of war, did you undertake any actions regarding the forensic analysis of the documents in order to double-check the things that seemed odd to you or not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe these -- this collection of documents was submitted to what could be called forensic analysis. The efforts to assess the veracity and the authenticity consisted of my efforts to compare them with other sources and compare them with what witnesses had told us, to seek to get the original copies or to seek -- we continued to seek archive access for a number of years, and to assess the contents -- it was an assessment of the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What do you believe that your expertise is based on when we're talking about the analysis of such documentation? Is it the experience that you gradually acquired working on documents, or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that my ability to analyse documents about -- military-related documents or documents about armed organisations was developed from -- during my time as an intelligence officer in the army, where I was working in a division and brigade headquarters. And in those headquarters I understood how divisions and brigades work, how the staffs operate, the commanders function, what types of reports are generated by lower units, such as daily combat reports. I understood how militaries function. And then at the ICTY as I studied the documentation on the VJ, with my background in military, I came to understand through the documentation how the VJ and also the MUP operated, how it was -- how both of them were structured, what reports they would generate, and the regulations within which and the laws within which they were bound to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: These experiences were acquired in the Canadian Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic experience in understanding how military functions certainly began in the Canadian Army; but as I mentioned, as I studied the documentation of the Army of Yugoslavia and the MUP of Serbia I could draw on that background to interpret those documents. And as an intelligence officer in the military I also understood our own military function from working in it. But our task was also -- it was - the Cold War still existed - was to study and work on eastern European and former Soviet Union militaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Responding to questions from my learned colleague Mr. Hannis yesterday you talked about a commission of the Army of Yugoslavia which was set up for purposes of cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. Do you know who formed the commission?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who was at the head of the Army of Yugoslavia at that time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain, but I believe General Pavkovic formed the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall any of the members of the commission who were also witnesses in the Milutinovic case?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't again remember for certain any names. I believe General Djakovic was on the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
