utterances.text: That is correct, thank you. I'm just briefly going to deal with the confiscations or seizure missions of documents, and we're talking about the IFOR and the SFOR missions in Bosnia. You referred to the doctrine of the Army of Yugoslavia and similar documents in those seizure missions. I don't know when this took place and was it really necessary in view of the accessibility of those documents on the part of Serbia. What did you mean when you talked about that particular aspect of document collection?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina the international force there, initially IFOR and then SFOR, conducted seizure missions. And I'm not familiar because I didn't work on those cases, I'm not familiar with the details of these seizure missions. Some of them were done on behalf of the OTP, some of them for IFOR and SFOR's own purposes, but in the process -- and some of these seizure missions had members of the OTP on them. In the process a large number of documents were collected and I believe have been used in other cases for the 1992 to 1995 conflict. For Kosovo there really wasn't much of relevance in those collections, with the exception of some doctrinal manuals from the JNA. We sought to verify whether or not these had been superseded by VJ manuals, and at the time we were having -- we weren't getting any cooperation from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Eventually we talked to some witnesses and we continued asking for doctrinal manuals through RFAs to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and successor states and came to the conclusion that most of these manuals were still applicable, they hadn't been updated and replaced with VJ manuals. We had one manual on command and control that was a VJ manual from 1996, I believe, and that was a manual which -- which was used at their General Staff college. The other assessment was that even if these manuals had been updated, what they were saying were very basic principles of command and control that it was assessed would be very unlikely to change, such as the responsibility of a commander and having a single chain of command. It just wouldn't be very plausible for such basics of military command to change from the JNA to the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We're now moving to the assistance requests sent to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. When, according to your information, does the cooperation between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and The Hague Prosecutor's office begin? Because you said earlier that at that time the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was not cooperating with the OTP, with The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it could be called cooperation, and I'm not really placed to conclude or assess that, but during the Milosevic case there was a 54 bis proceeding which was quite lengthy, the outcome of which was the issuance of some Court orders to Serbia and Montenegro -- or perhaps it was still the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to comply with some the -- some aspects of the RFAs from the OTP. And there was some compliance with those at that point, but it wasn't until 2006 when we gained access to the archives that I would consider cooperation to be anything approaching full cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the law on the cooperation with The Hague Tribunal was adopted in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the body called the Council for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal was established?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I believe it was sometime during the Milosevic trial, if not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now we're going to go back to a very important subject, the archives of the army and the MUP. You talked about that -- well, now we're talking about 2006 and the mission when you -- when a part of the team arrived in May and the other part arrived in August, as you said, and you reviewed documents, and that you received replies pursuant to your RFAs in September and some in November. However, what I'm interested in is -- well, were you there in May 2006, in that team? First tell me that.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now that is quite clear. Can you please tell me -- for example, you said that the MUP furnished this documentation in September and the Army of Yugoslavia in November of the same year. After that you said that the way the Army of Yugoslavia archived its document was quite proper and well done, compared to the MUP way of archiving. What exactly did you mean when you said that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia had an archive which was of the size that I would expect for such an organisation. It was -- it had to be relocated because the original location had been bombed by NATO, so it was in the basement of a school or academy in Belgrade at the time we went -- the first time we went. They had proper archive registers, and when those registers were reviewed by us within the archive or the temporary archive we would ask for -- to see a particular document and very quickly they could bring us the document. There was a very systematic way of documenting their information. They had millions of pages of archive materials. They had professional archivists, at least the people we met, that's what I was led to believe was their function and background. In the MUP, in contrast, we were taken to a room or two rooms next to each other in the headquarters in Belgrade, and we were shown what they called the dossier KiM or the dossier Kosovo and Metohija. And it was explained to us that this was a compilation put together on General Lukic's instruction of all the materials that they considered relevant to Kosovo. So in that respect I wouldn't consider that an archive. And we never did see anything in the MUP that I would have considered an archive in the terms that I understand an archive, a very systematic -- systematically ordered and formal system for keeping documents that have been archived in accordance with archiving regulations. What we saw was a collection that had been put together for a specific purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when General Lukic ordered the forming of the KiM dossier? Was that in 2001?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what function General Lukic held at that time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that when we -- General Lukic was the head of the public security department of the MUP at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And what about General Djordjevic at the time, at the time when General Lukic was the chief of the service, do you know what his position was at that time before the indictment was ever issued? Did you ever dwell upon that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the precise date when General Djordjevic left his position as head of the public security service of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember the conditions under which he left? Were you ever interested in that as you were working on this case, as I see you were?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the details of the conditions. I was primarily concerned with 1999 and 1998. I know that -- or I believe that he fled around about the time that allegations of the hiding of bodies and the refrigerator truck were surfacing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you only think that, or do you know this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the -- my best recollection. So I'm not absolutely certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know what function was held by General Djordjevic before he left MUP? Do you know the exact title of that function or position? What was his position in the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last position that I'm certain of him holding, whether or not it was the last position in the MUP, was the head of the RJB, which is the public security department of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the minister of the interior, what was his position or role vis-a-vis the minister of the interior? Do you know that? Was he his assistant or his deputy, to be more precise? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to review the Law on Internal Affairs, but -- and again I've seen it sometimes translated as assistant and sometimes deputy, but I believe it's assistant to the minister, and there were a number of other assistants to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How come that in some reports he's referred to as deputy minister, which he never was? I agree with you on that.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It could be that it's a translation issue. I know that there were two components to the MUP: The public security department and the state security department, the RDB. And the two heads reported to the minister. And under each of the respective heads there were a number of assistant ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the accused would like to consult with me, so I will ask your leave to allow me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, Mr. Coo, I understand that you cannot be very precise in remembering the organisation without reviewing your notes. So when it comes to the structure of the MUP, I believe that we have not obtained the most precise answers from you. I will not dwell upon the issue, though the only thing I'm interested in now is the basis of your faith in public sources. I'm referring to the press, the internet, web presentations by the ministry, the army, and the police. And I'm also referring to the dailies, magazines, different comments and different interviews, different other sources, although you never knew whether any authorisation was obtained for publication from the person with whom the interview was allegedly conducted. What is the probative value that you assign to such sources? How do you see such sources? How do you interpret them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an objection to the portion of the question about asking this witness what probative value he assigns to certain items. I think that's an ultimate question for Your Honours and not for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't agree with you, Mr. Hannis. I think the question is proper. What was being asked is what probative value did this witness attach, and I think that's a proper approach. Carry on, please, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to repeat my question, or can you answer it without me repeating it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's fine, I understood the question. The probative value would depend on -- and the value generally that I gave to an open or a public source would depend on the source, and I'd have to see each one. But in general terms I wouldn't accept such a source in isolation. It was always integrated in the analysis with corroborative sources, generally official documents. If the source was official, such as the Vojska magazine produced for the VJ, by the VJ, I would attach more value to that -- certainly that it had been at least authorised by the VJ and the contents screened by the VJ. If it was a newspaper, I might attach less -- or be less certain of the contents or statements but certainly attempt and would feel more reassured about what was being said if the contents were corroborated by other independently acquired, especially official, information. So in general terms I think open sources or public sources could have some probative value.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will bring my today's examination to an end with the following question: Do you know that the central archive building of the Ministry of the Interior was also bombed in a NATO campaign which started on the 24th of March, 1999. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that the MUP headquarters in Belgrade was bombed, but we always maintained that when we were told in response to RFAs that documents had been destroyed in that bombing, the documentation that we were seeking would not have been archived by that time. It would still be with the units that were producing the documents. So in that regard we didn't accept the reasoning given that because the archives or the MUP headquarters had been destroyed that the documents of interest to us had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally inspect those buildings? Not only the central MUP building in Kneza Milosa Street, but also those buildings which were bombed outside the capital in other towns and places? Do you have any personal knowledge of the destruction? Did you visit those buildings or not? Can you tell us something about that.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited some of the MUP or SUP headquarters in Kosovo, not outside Kosovo. We knew that the SUPs and other units had moved out of these buildings when NATO bombing began under -- with the knowledge that they would be primary targets for NATO. But we were never told that the MUP had kept archived documents in other places in Serbia. We were essentially told that the -- all of the available documents that we were seeking were in the dossier KiM or in some of the offices of different units, such as the border police in parts of Belgrade, which -- and we did visit those offices on subsequent missions and came across only a handful of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions for you. I believe that we have received enough answers, including the answer about the documentation, whether it was destroyed in the NATO campaign or not. It seems that your knowledge is not reliable, that it is more --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour to that commentary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you know better than that. What your views are about the reliability is not the sort of thing you can make an observation about. In due course you will be able to put submissions to us on the evidence. Mr. Hannis, do you re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I have a few questions, Your Honour. I'd like to start with P887 and D204. These are the documents that Mr. Djordjevic had a question about at page -- starting at page 26 today. And I guess for -- if it's possible, if we could have both English versions up for Mr. Coo side by side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, I think you'll remember this discussion. One is the order from General Ojdanic, and it's on the left side of the screen; and on the right is the related order from General Pavkovic. I will -- and the document on the right, which is sign -- has a signature and a stamp from General Pavkovic, you'll see above the signature block the initials MDj and BV. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis is kindly asked to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And General Djakovic testified here and indicated to us that the MDj were his initials as the author of that document. Were you familiar with that manner of notations in VJ documents?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I believe that the first initial was the authorising officer and the second would be the drafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djordjevic asked you a question about the registry numbers at the top of each of these. General Pavkovic's on the right is 872-94/1 and the one on the left is 872-94/2. What do you know about the numbering system within the 3rd Army and Pristina Corps in 1999? What do you understand about how documents were assigned numbers like this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that the 872, the first three digits, would be related to the -- it was either the unit or the subject. So, for example, operations -- operational related information might have a particular three-digit number. The second part of the number after the dash I believe was -- although I'm not fully familiar with the system, General Vasiljevic explained part of it at one point. But I believe it's a sequential numbering system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the stroke 1, stroke 2, does that indicate anything about those two documents and the relationship with each other?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure, but I believe they're different copies -- they reflect the different copies of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you learn anything in the course of your work about how these numbers were assigned within the Pristina Corps or the 3rd Army? Who gave the document a number and when was the number attached to the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it was my understanding that the numbers would be assigned by a clerk essentially, who would be responsible for the dissemination of the document, not the drafting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know at what point in time that clerk would put the number on the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for sure whether it was before or after the document had been signed. I believe it was after when it was being registered by the clerk in the unit's register.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And apart from these two documents, do you have any other evidence to support that General Ojdanic indeed did issue such an order on or about the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There was the -- the order from the -- not the order but a report from the 2nd Army at the same time making reference to the same General Staff order about subordination of the MUP to the VJ. There was -- there were some other orders, one in fact in 25th of May, I believe, from the 3rd Army discussing the issue of subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And with regard to General Pavkovic's order, in essence relaying the order on down to subordinates, did you have other documentation from other sources suggesting that that indeed had occurred on or about that day?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall for certain. I think some of the brigades reflected the -- the Pristina Corps reflected this in its own order and some of the Pristina Corps brigades followed up, so the chain of command issued a sequence of orders regarding the subordination of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was more general discussion about the whole issue of the subordination of the MUP within -- within the VJ's documentation, and it was also certainly mentioned by witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Now let me turn to another subject at page 39 today, line 16. Mr. Djordjevic was asking you about missing documents, and you specifically mentioned the Pristina Corps war diary. What can you tell us about that? Where -- where from your knowledge of how archiving was done in the VJ after the war would you have expected to find the Pristina Corps war diary?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the time we got to the archives in 2006, that war diary should have been in the archives of the VJ in Belgrade. And under the archiving regulations, because it was produced during a state of war, should have been kept permanently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when it was not there, did you make inquiries and what were you told?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did make inquiries, and they simply didn't know. They said the war diary, there's no record of that war diary having been submitted to the archives. General Lazarevic was asked during his interview and also failed to account for the location of the war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what he specifically said about it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And lastly, the question concerning your view on the probative value of some of the documents from public or non-official sources. The documents that were on your provenance list that were part of the supporting materials in the reports that you wrote concerning the Kosovo conflict, some of those include internet sources or newspaper or magazine articles. Did you ever rely for any of the points written in your report solely on an unofficial public source?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no other questions, Your Honour. I do have one administrative matter, if I may, though. With regard to Exhibit P1289, which was marked for identification, that was one of the documents related to the RFAs, the translation has been located. It's been disclosed to the Defence. I believe the Registry officer has it now, and we would ask if it can be attached and admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, that has been marked for identification, pending translation. The translation now provided may be attached and it will become an exhibit of the same number. Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Coo, you'll be pleased to know that that completes the questions for you. The Chamber would thank you for your attendance and your assistance. You may of course now resume your normal activities and a Court Officer will show you out when we rise, which will be in a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, does the question of the written submission you want to make about the various documents, what time do you feel you would need for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two to three weeks would be enough for us to submit our written submission with regard to the list that I have before me. So the break should suffice for us to do so in order to explain things, as we already announced during the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Secondly, I would kindly ask my learned friend, Mr. Hannis, to submit an updated list because some of the evidence was withdrawn from the list after our objections. For example, the Law on the Ministry of the Interior, which is no longer valid. This would allow us to be more precise with regard to the admitted evidence. There were some additional documents outside of the notice that we previously had, so this is my other request with regard to the administrative matters in these proceedings. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll certainly do that, Your Honour. I think there were only two we dropped from the original list, but I also have the list of the VJ collegiums and we'll provide that to the Registry officer and Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How long will that take you, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we could have it to him by Monday, if not the end of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you can do that. Mr. Djordjevic, I think we should allow you the time after you get that list, so we will ask that you provide your written submissions within two weeks of next Monday, so you have two weeks after next -- from next Monday to provide the submissions. Thank you very much. We will now adjourn and we resume on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 31st day of August, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.28 p.m.,
